title: State-dependent coupling: resonant memory to narrow-channel learning
summary: September 25-26 turns the resonant-brain note into three progressively harsher tests. ResonaattoriAivo shows that a clock-slaved resonator memory can transfer melodies across tempo from one training tempo and that plastic response geometry can rescue noisy memory, while its state-dependent event-shape stage fails to show transfer of old history. FridayRepo isolates the two-sided interaction—sender history changes an emitted temporal shape while receiver history changes susceptibility—and shows that the supplied factorization is learnable, then corrects the literal query-time story when a generic RNN often compiles the joint answer before the common query. KapeaKanava removes the comfortable single-system setting: two learners must communicate old history through a small noisy message. Generic pairs mostly fail to bootstrap communication; a multiplicative interface helps learning start and reaches the task rank bound when it does, while a cheap shortcut captures the channel and history is carried in 0 of 36 shortcut runs. The surviving object is therefore narrower than 'resonant brain': state-dependent coupling is a useful inductive bias and response geometry matters, but communication startup and shortcut competition are the current bottlenecks.

nodes.claim: Tests a beat-coordinate resonator sequence memory, then asks whether prediction residue can retune the response geometry under noise and whether state-dependent event shape can carry history between modules.
nodes.survived: Trained at one tempo, the clock-slaved model averaged 94.8% next-beat accuracy across 0.6x-1.6x tempo, while freezing the clock cost about 48 points; free-run recall averaged 97.3% across tempos. Under state noise 0.01, retuning only 16 resonator decay/frequency parameters raised whole-song accuracy from 58.7% fixed to 88.3% across three fresh seeds. This supports tempo-normalized temporal coordinates and plastic response geometry as useful mechanisms in the toy.
nodes.killed: The primary slow-band context gate failed, and slow modes were fragile under noise. Once the much larger mode-to-pyramid coupling was trainable, retuning resonator frequencies/decays added no measurable gain, so the useful plasticity is not uniquely a resonance-frequency effect. Stage 3 also failed to show old history crossing in event shape: a short-memory sender gave the same gain and sender-history transplants rarely redirected continuation. The event shape is abstract, not a biological action-potential model.

nodes.claim: Isolates whether hidden sender history can alter an emitted temporal shape while hidden receiver history alters susceptibility, so identical event times can lead to different continuations; then removes supplied state labels and finally the explicit factorization.
nodes.survived: The known-answer waveform-times-susceptibility construction reached 97.84% while timestamp, clamped/shuffled waveform, fixed-receiver and additive attackers stayed at about chance. A learned state-conditioned susceptibility reached 96.05% +/- 0.62%, and the learned-history factorized model reached 95.00% +/- 0.96% using only continuation error. In the generic 12-unit RNN falsifier, 4 of 8 initializations solved and those solved runs reached 97.34% +/- 1.57% held out, showing that ordinary nonlinear recurrent dynamics can also compile the history interaction.
nodes.killed: The first construction is a known-answer bilinear mechanism, and the learned-history version still supplies the sender-shape x receiver-susceptibility factorization. In the generic-dynamics falsifier, every solved run already had the joint answer linearly decodable before the identical query (97.27% +/- 1.62%), so the result does not show that a generic learner invented a waveform/susceptibility interface or that the query created the interaction. It does not establish a biological resonance or action-potential communication code.

nodes.claim: Tests whether two separately learned systems connected only by a small noisy message can bootstrap history-dependent interaction, reach the known low-rank channel bound, use the channel minimally, and keep carrying history when a cheap shortcut competes for capacity.
nodes.survived: The direct ceiling solved all target ranks at R^2 0.995-0.998. Generic receivers could compute the interaction when handed an oracle message, but sender-receiver co-learning rarely started; a bilinear interface started much more reliably. Whenever a bilinear run did start, its best seed closely tracked the k/r rank bound, including 0.499/0.5, 0.328/0.333 and 0.655/0.667. At high noise, active message dimensions collapsed to the target rank without an explicit sparsity cost, and spare channel dimensions could materially improve startup.
nodes.killed: Generic sender-receiver pairs mostly failed to bootstrap communication, especially as rank and noise increased. An explicit message-energy penalty often made the startup deadlock worse rather than enforcing a useful minimal code. Most sharply, when a cheap recent-context shortcut was present, old history was carried in 0 of 36 runs: the shortcut reached about 0.91-0.97 uptake and the history interaction stayed near zero even with spare dimensions. The study uses three seeds per main cell, small GRUs and abstract vectors rather than biological waveforms.

edges.why: FridayRepo takes the unresolved interface exposed by ResonaattoriAivo Stage 3—state-dependent event shape helped, but did not demonstrably carry old history—and isolates the stronger two-sided question: sender history controls temporal publication while receiver history controls how that publication is read.

KapeaKanava explicitly grows out of FridayRepo and removes the comfortable supplied single-system factorization: two learners must discover a useful message through a narrow noisy channel, exposing communication startup as a separate problem from interaction computability.

KapeaKanava explicitly names ResonaattoriAivo Stage 3 as a parent. It turns that stage's failure to demonstrate old-history transfer through event shape into a controlled communication test with exact-rank tasks, channel-width sweeps and a cheap shortcut attacker.
